title: Exhaust fan window mount + removable dovetail joint (Fusion 360, OrcaSlicer, Claude)
goal: Design the window mount for the exhaust fan: a 2-piece design where one part is permanently fixed to the window and reverse-engineers the dimensions of an Arctic P12 PWM computer fan into a housing with a grille/diffuser, and the second part is a temporary removable joint connecting that housing to the session-1 table mount.
context: This is the 2nd part of the same project carried out in session 1. I am planning to design the window mount for the exhaust fan. Here I am going to reverse engineer the dimensions of a computer fan, make it seat in a housing which will be mounted on the window for exhaust of 3D printer fumes. It is a 2 piece design where 1 part is permanently fixed on the window and the other part is a temporary joint with the design carried out in session 1.

session_goal_achievement.Why or why not: Step 1 & 2 took the most time where I had to clarify things 2-3 times and also had to assume a few design features and dimensions by myself (for eg. it didn’t account for the tolerance required to mount the exhaust vent, claude answer-106mm, needed answer-104mm). Rest of the steps went smoothly.

Step 1.step_name: Get design inputs from Claude for both mountings and sketch the fan-seat in Autodesk Fusion
Step 1.step_action: Describe the fan/hose/window grille specs to Claude and request a dimensioned outline for the fan-to-duct adapter and window diffuser/grille mount.

nodes.label: Ask for design and dimensions for an exhaust-fan mount. Design the window mount in Fusion 360, working through repeated dimensional corrections with Claude.
nodes.detail: The participant opens a new Claude chat ('Ender 3 exhaust fan window mount design') and writes a project brief: an Arctic P12 Slim PWM PST fan, a 4-inch aluminum exhaust hose, and an 80x80mm window grille made of 10mm-wide square bars. Specifies the design must be 2 parts: a fan-to-hose adapter and a diffuser to keep exhaust from blowing back through the grille into the room.

nodes.label: Web-search Arctic P12 Slim PWM fan dimensions
nodes.detail: Claude runs several web searches to pin down the real Arctic P12 Slim PWM PST fan dimensions before proposing anything. The user interrupts the generation.

nodes.label: Launch Autodesk Fusion
Interrupt Claude and edit the prompt to request a design made using '\,|,/,_ ' and mention the dimensions for side view, top view, etc.
Interrupt Claude and edit the prompt to ask Claude to skip printing recommendations and only give the design based on proper dimensions
Propose initial 2-part fan-to-duct adapter + anti-backflow diffuser hood design with key dimensions, side view, and front view
nodes.detail: Claude proposes the requested two-part design: Part 1 is a fan-to-duct adapter (120x120mm flange, 4x M4 holes at 105x105mm pitch, tapering from a 115mm bore to a 98mm duct spigot); Part 2 is a baffle/diffuser with a 180x180mm outlet covering a 2x2 grille block and an angled baffle plate for airflow.

nodes.label: Review the design and ask for changes
nodes.detail: The participant reviews the design and asks for changes to have cutouts and holes to mount the fan and on the wall, and a 90 degree bend for mounting the exhaust hose with recommended dimensions

nodes.label: Propose section-by-section dimensions
Review the design, load the previous design of the enclosure side mount in Autodesk Fusion to check the inner diameter of the exhaust hose, and edit the prompt to add the diameter.
nodes.softwares: Autodesk Fusion 360; Claude (chat, Sonnet 5, web search enabled)

nodes.label: Redraw combined design, adopt 106mm hose-ID assumption
nodes.detail: Claude re-derives the design as a single integrated part (fan seat to 90-degree bend to wall flange) across several iterations. The participant's message includes the instruction 'Assume exhaust hose inner dia is 106mm,' and Claude locks this 106mm figure in as the bend/duct bore size that will be carried through all subsequent dimensioning.

nodes.label: Sketch fan-seat in AutodeskFusion, using the dimensions from Claude's proposal in a10
nodes.detail: The participant opens Fusion 360, browses the existing 'Enclosure side mount' and 'Table Side mount' files from session 1 for reference, then starts a new sketch: a 120x120mm square fan-seat plate with a large circular bore (confirmed on screen ~00:20:40 with the same reference files visible in the Data panel).

nodes.label: Read Claude's suggested dimensions and report printer calibration error, ask for clearances
Deliver a compensation table for the printer calibration error
Read suggested dimensions, and ask for features that Claude missed: fan-seat, wall mount should be larger, etc. And ask about the feasibility of the accomodating the taper within the bend.
Confirm taper feasibility, correct wall foot sizing, and update L-hole pattern
nodes.detail: Claude confirms the taper is feasible at a shallow ~1.3-1.6 degree half-angle, shrinks the bend centerline radius from 130mm to 100mm for compactness, and continues sizing the whole bend/duct bore to the 106mm hose-ID figure established earlier in Step 1 -- carrying that assumption through the taper and bend math without re-checking it.

nodes.label: Model fan seat and foot plate in Fusion 360
nodes.detail: The participant switches to Fusion 360 and builds the fan-seat pocket with the 115mm bore (measuring a 12.5mm wall between the fan seat and outer rim), then sketches the 140mm wall-foot outline around the 120mm fan seat, briefly flipping back to Claude's print-compensated values and updated envelope table while modeling.

nodes.label: Ask for pitch for the wall-holes
nodes.detail: While modeling, the participant asks for the wall-hole pitch ('give me only the dimension'); Claude answers 100mm, and the participant pushes back ('how is it 100mm? the fan housing itself is 120mm') and catches a real geometric error: Claude's 140x140mm foot plate had the fan centered inside it, so the mounting holes actually landed underneath the fan body rather than being screwdriver-accessible outside it ('the foot (where it is mounted onto the wall) sits outside the fan housing').

nodes.label: Propose the holes should be 100mm (98.5mm compensated for the printer)
Tell Claude 100mm is absolutely wrong because the fan housing itself is 120mm
Explain the reason for the 100mm pitch
Correct Claude that the foot sits outside the fan housing
Propose corrected dimensions for the pitch
Read Claude's corrected dimensions for the pitch

Step 2.step_action: Design the window mount in Fusion 360, working through repeated dimensional corrections with Claude.

nodes.label: Sketch the bend in Fusion
Sketch the hose-side lip/slot and save the file
nodes.detail: The participant exports the fan-mount part (visible as 'Exhaust Fan mounting' in the Fusion data panel) and closes out this part of the session, telling Claude 'Ok that part is over, thanks for your help'.

nodes.label: Report to Claude that the fan window mounting part is done
Confirm the part is done
Confirm the part is done

Step 3.step_action: Design the removable joint in Fusion 360, pivoting from a rejected bayonet concept to a dovetail-slide-with-latch mechanism.

nodes.label: Pivot to removable joint, attach fan-mount screenshot
nodes.detail: The participant pivots to the second part: 'Now onto the second part, I need a temporary removable joint which will clamp onto this part,' attaching a screenshot of the just-finished fan window mount and explaining it must also serve as a second, removable exhaust-hose attachment point for solder-fume extraction near the printer.

nodes.label: Propose bayonet twist-lock coupler and deliver infterface dimensions suggestions
nodes.detail: Claude proposes a bayonet-style twist-lock coupler: a skirt with 3 L-shaped slots and flex detent tabs on one part, mating lugs on the other, twisting ~18 degrees to lock -- preferred over a snap-fit clip because it tolerates the printer's calibration drift better than precision cantilever flex. The participant briefly Googles 'bayonet style twist lock' while reading.

nodes.label: Search on google about the bayonet twist-lock coupler
Rule out bayonet or anything requiring rotation, and ask for sliding parts
nodes.detail: The participant explicitly rules the bayonet out: 'look closer, the image i have given has ribs on the side, so there is no possibility or space for twisting anything, the part can be attached only by' sliding -- the part sits flush against a ribbed/rimmed surface with no room to turn.

nodes.label: Pivot to dovetail-slide-with-latch design
nodes.detail: Claude pivots to a dovetail slide with a positive latch, explicitly compared to a GoPro quick-release plate: the mating part slides down vertically onto rails, seats against a stop ridge, and a single spring-tab latch clicks into a pocket to lock -- avoiding any rotation clearance requirement.

nodes.label: Ask whether the joint will be leak-proof
nodes.detail: The participant asks a pointed follow-up: 'will these be leak proof', then, while Claude responds, Googles images of 'printed dovetail joint with latch'.

nodes.label: Diagnose leak paths, propose foam gasket fix
nodes.detail: Claude answers 'no, not as designed' -- the dovetail slide is a mechanical joint, not a sealed one -- identifies the flat backplate-to-face contact as the main leak path, and proposes a 3mm closed-cell foam gasket ring at the backplate interface, noting the latch's clamping force is exactly what's needed to compress it properly.

nodes.label: Search on google about spigot and the dovetail-slide-with-latch design
nodes.detail: The participant looks over the table-side mount in Fusion 360 and re-reads Claude's dovetail rail cross-section, then runs a Google Images search for 'go pro quick release' to visually confirm the quick-release mechanism Claude had described, before returning to the chat.

nodes.label: Search on google about go pro quick release design, and ask for the dimensions of the dovetail, restrcting the depth to 3-4mm max
nodes.softwares: Claude (chat, Sonnet 5, web search enabled), Browser

nodes.label: Relax dovetail dims for shallow cutout, providing dimensions for the rail and the socket
nodes.detail: Claude confirms 3-4mm is workable since dovetail retention comes from the flare angle rather than depth, and shrinks the rail cross-section to a 5mm neck and 9mm head at 3.2mm total height (still labeled '30 degree flare'), offering 3.0mm or 3.5mm socket-pocket depths in the 6mm plate.

nodes.label: Ask for the dovetail's actual angle
nodes.detail: The participant asks 'back to the earlier dovetail, what is the angle?', catching that Claude had been repeating a label without checking it against the actual geometry.

nodes.label: Correct mislabeled 30 degree angle to actual 45 degrees
nodes.detail: Claude recalculates from the stated neck/head dimensions (8mm neck, 14mm flared head over a 3mm height) and finds the earlier '30 degree' label didn't match the geometry it had actually drawn -- the real angle is 45 degrees per side, which it confirms is a standard, GoPro-style dovetail angle. The participant then sketches the 8mm/14mm dovetail profile in Fusion 360.

nodes.label: Sketch the dovetail profile in Fusion 360
Asks for a dovetail with 3mm height and 9mm longer side
nodes.detail: The participant locks in final dovetail dimensions ('give me a dovetail, 3mm height is fine, longer side should be 9mm')

nodes.label: Propose a dovetail with 3mm height and 9mm longer side
nodes.detail: Claude proposes a dovetail with 3mm height and 9mm longer side

nodes.label: Proposes to scale up to 4-6 sets of dovetails
Flag 6-rail plan as alignment risk, propose segmented teeth
nodes.detail: Claude flags going from 2 rails to 6 fully independent rails as a real feasibility risk given the printer's known +1.5% scaling error -- 6 independent alignment points would likely bind or fail to reach. It proposes instead keeping the existing 2 rail lines but segmenting each 60mm rail into 3 short 14mm teeth with 9mm gaps, giving 6 engagement points while keeping only the original 2 axes of alignment.

nodes.label: Sketch the 6 dovetail rails in Fusion 360 and save the files

Step 4.step_name: Prepare files for 3D printing in OrcaSlicer
Step 4.step_action: Upload the designed files in OrcaSlicer, take slicing parameters from Claude, and slice both design files.

nodes.label: Make screenshots of the attachment to table mount and exhaust fan mount design and ask claude for print orientation and parameters for slicing in orcaslicer
nodes.softwares: Claude (chat, Sonnet 5, web search enabled), Autodesk Fusion 360

nodes.label: Propose print orientation and parameters for slicing in orcaslicer
nodes.detail: Working from the screenshots, Claude recommends the ring/toothed base plate print flat with the ring standing vertical (0-degree overhang walls, no supports needed) and specifies settings for both parts: 0.20mm layer height, 4 wall loops, 20-25% grid/gyroid infill, and a 5mm brim to fight warping on the thin ring wall.

nodes.label: Export the attachment to table mount and exhaust fan mount design to STL files, launch OrcaSlicer, import attachment to table mount STL
Import exhaust fan mount STL, rotate and move it, adjust print parameters according to Claude's suggestions

Step 5.step_name: Refine design and parameters for print time optimization
Step 5.step_action: Further optimize slicer settings and the design geometry to reduce material usage and print time.

nodes.label: Report excessive support/print-time, ask for optimization
nodes.detail: Report that part 2 needs 1.44 kg of support material and ask for optimization

nodes.label: Diagnose the swept bend as root cause, propose rotation
nodes.detail: Claude diagnoses that the swept 90-degree bend round-face-down is generating the excessive support volume (which is not true because the user doesn't adopt the round-face-down design that claude proposed earlier), and proposes to change to flange-down design.

nodes.label: Save the attachment to table mount to gcode file, start slicing the exhaust fan mount
Adjust print parameters to reduce time and weight, and tell Claude the time target of 12-18 hours and the weight target of 150g-200g
Propose splitting the elbow at the bend apexinto two parts and setting changes on top of the split
Iterate OrcaSlicer passes chasing the time/weight target
nodes.detail: The participant runs several more OrcaSlicer passes at Draft 0.28mm quality, toggling support type between Tree and Organic, adjusting branch density and threshold angle, and lowering sparse infill to as little as 12% gyroid, watching the estimate drop from the initial multi-day figure through intermediate readings (confirmed on screen: ~2d5h/252g, then ~14h8m in-progress).

nodes.label: Export final gcode -- time target met, weight target missed
nodes.detail: The session ends with the final gcode exported and visible on screen: 'Exhuast Fan mounting_PLA_14h9m.gcode' at 252.21g and 14h9m total print time, with the support line-item now negligible after the elbow split. This is a partial, imperfect outcome: the ~16-hour print-time target from the doc's own rubric is met, but the final weight lands above the 150g material target -- matching the doc's own honest assessment that print time 'could have minimised further.'
